questions.prompt: For digits 23 and dictionary [ad, ae, be, cf, dg], which result obeys the closed-dictionary contract?

options.label: Return [ad, ae, be, cf]; only complete dictionary words with the exact encoding qualify.
Return all nine letter pairs, even when absent from the dictionary.
Return dg because the dictionary is trusted, regardless of its encoding.

questions.explanation: The accepted words encode to 23 and are complete dictionary members. Generating all pairs ignores membership; dg encodes to 34, so trusting a dictionary does not remove the encoding check.

questions.prompt: The trie contains ad and adg. What should query 23 return?

options.label: Return only ad for 23; adg is a longer word, and an unfinished prefix is not a result.
Return both words because their prefix matches.
Return no words because a terminal node must have no children.

questions.explanation: Emit only a terminal node after every digit is consumed. adg needs another digit; a terminal node may also have children, so it is valid to store both a short and longer word.

questions.prompt: Query 22 searches aa, ab and ba using one mutable buffer. Which ownership rule is correct?

options.label: Snapshot each completed word and pop the chosen letter before exploring the next sibling.
Save the buffer object itself so every result can reuse storage.
Keep a global visited-letter set to forbid using a twice.

questions.explanation: Snapshot a string so results survive later mutations, and undo the branch choice before a sibling. Sharing the buffer corrupts saved results; a global letter ban rejects legitimate repeated-position words such as aa.

questions.prompt: Digits are empty or no trie prefix matches, but a dictionary entry is uppercase or empty. What should happen?

options.label: Reject the malformed dictionary before search, even when digits are empty or no prefix matches.
Return an empty result immediately because no output is expected.
Silently normalize or drop malformed words before building the trie.

questions.explanation: The whole input contract must be validated before any empty-query or no-match shortcut. An early success bypasses the contract; silent normalization changes the authored ASCII policy and can conceal incorrect input.

questions.prompt: A trie passes the bounded oracle. Is it now the fastest choice for every query?

options.label: Compare with the independent scan under the same input contract; measure repeated-query costs before preferring a trie.
Yes: prefix pruning removes every construction and output-copying cost.
Yes: 340 bounded patterns prove correctness and speed for arbitrary dictionaries.

questions.explanation: The independent scan provides a separate correctness reference on valid inputs. Trie construction and copying still cost work, and finite checks do not prove arbitrary-input correctness or performance. Choose from measured workload and ownership needs.
